vision_features.image_context: A field-level view of a soybean crop row showing multiple whole plants. The image captures a gap or stand failure zone in the middle of the row between two flanking groups of healthy plants. Both plant-level and canopy-level context are visible. Bare sandy/loamy soil is exposed in the central area.
vision_features.abnormalities: 1. Central gap zone — spanning approximately 60–80 cm along the row: Several plants in the center of the row are severely stunted and collapsed compared to neighboring plants. Their stems are thin, dark brown to black in color from the soil line upward, with a dry, shriveled texture. Leaves on these affected plants are shrunken, curled, and have turned tan to light brown, appearing dry and papery. The tissue collapse appears to originate at or just below the soil surface and extends up the lower stem. 2. Fallen/lodged stems: Multiple stems in the central zone are lying flat on the soil surface, appearing to have lost structural integrity at the base. They are dark brown to blackish, dry, and thin. 3. Leaf tissue on affected plants: Leaves range from pale yellowish-green to fully tan/brown and dry. They are small, crinkled, and some have dropped to the soil. No large distinct marks or spots are visible on individual leaves; the entire leaf surface appears uniformly discolored and desiccated. 4. Soil surface in the gap: Bare, dry, sandy-colored soil is exposed, with scattered dead plant debris lying on it. 5. Transition zone: Plants immediately adjacent to the gap show slightly reduced vigor — some lower leaves appear pale or light green — but upper canopy leaves on flanking plants appear healthy and dark green.
vision_features.absences: 1. No powdery or dusty coating is visible on any leaf surfaces or stems. 2. No raised bumps, pustules, or blister-like structures are visible on stems or leaves. 3. No visible insect bodies, webbing, or feeding damage holes on the remaining leaf tissue. 4. No water-soaked or slimy appearance on any of the affected tissue; all damaged material appears dry.
vision_features.summary: The image shows a soybean field with a localized stand failure zone in the center of a row, where multiple plants have collapsed and died while flanking plants remain largely healthy and green. Affected plants display dark brown to black discoloration and shrinkage of stems starting at or near the soil line, with complete drying and browning of associated leaf tissue. Several stems have lost structural support and are lying flat on the bare soil. The most severely affected organ is the lower stem at the soil interface, and the single most striking visual feature is the abrupt, localized death of plants within a confined section of the row, creating a clear gap in the otherwise intact canopy.

Available classes in 'Soybean_Diseases' (5 total):

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phytophthora':
────────────────────────────────────────
Young plants show rapid yellowing and wilting with soft rot and collapse of the root. Mature plants exhibit general yellowing of lower leaves progressing upward, followed by wilting and death, with brown discolored roots and a dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending from below the soil line upward several nodes; leaves typically stay attached after plant death.. The best diagnostic symptom on susceptible varieties is a lower stem discoloration (dark chocolate-brown) that may extend several nodes up the stem. Root system shows lateral and branch roots almost completely discolored; tap roots with brown surface discoloration and tan to brown inner tissue discoloration. Leaves turn yellow, wilt, and typically stay attached after plant death.. stem canker, Pythium
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Diaporthe':
────────────────────────────────────────
Parallel rows of black, flask-shaped specks or pycnidia on mature soybean stems occurring later in the season (R6 to R8 growth stages). Pycnidia may also develop on dry, poorly developed pods, but may be dispersed randomly rather than arranged linearly.. Parallel rows of black, flask-shaped pycnidia arranged linearly on stems; random dispersal on pods.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phomopsis':
────────────────────────────────────────
Infected seed are cracked, shriveled, dull, and may have a gray mold on them.. Seed infected by pod and stem blight may decompose after harvest and have low viability; seedlings grown from infected seeds may often be blighted.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Bacterial_Blight':
────────────────────────────────────────
Infections begin as small, angular, water-soaked spots that turn yellow and then brown as the tissue dies. Lesions have dark reddish-brown centers surrounded by yellowish-green halos around water-soaked tissue; lesions may coalesce to form large, irregularly shaped lesions. Leaf veins may become affected creating necrotic areas resembling lightning on the leaf. Eventually lesions fall out leaving ragged foliage.. Presence of a yellowish-green halo around lesions; most common on young leaves in mid to upper canopy whereas brown spot is usually seen on older, lower leaves; lack of fungal structures in lesions.. Septoria brown spot, brown spot
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Green_stem_disorder':
────────────────────────────────────────
All or part of the soybean plant remains green while the rest of the plant or neighboring plants mature, most commonly seen in stems, leaves or pods; stems remain moist while pods and seeds have ripened.. Stems and occasionally leaves remain green and moist after pods and seeds have ripened and turned brown; excessive leaves on plant and green stems when neighboring plants are near harvest maturity.
────────────────────────────────────────

DISCRIMINATING: 'Diaporthe' vs 'Phytophthora'
Ruling feature : Presence of discrete black flask-shaped pycnidia in parallel rows on stems (Disease A) vs. dark chocolate-brown internal stem discoloration extending upward from the soil line with no pycnidia (Disease B)
Diaporthe: Mature stems display parallel linear rows of black, flask-shaped pycnidia (visible surface structures); pycnidia may also appear randomly on pods. Symptoms occur late in the season (R6–R8).
Phytophthora: Dark chocolate-brown discoloration of the lower stem extending from below the soil line upward several nodes, accompanied by brown/discolored roots, general yellowing of lower leaves progressing upward, wilting, and leaves remaining attached after plant death.
Decision rule  : IF you see distinct black flask-shaped pycnidia arranged in parallel rows on the stem surface, THEN diagnose Diaporthe (Disease A); IF the stem shows a dark chocolate-brown internal/external discoloration beginning at or below the soil line with no surface pycnidia and leaves remaining attached after death, THEN diagnose Phytophthora (Disease B).

DISCRIMINATING: 'Phomopsis' vs 'Phytophthora'
Ruling feature : Dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending upward from below the soil line (Phytophthora) vs. cracked, shriveled, gray-moldy seed with no stem/root discoloration described (Phomopsis)
Phomopsis: Phomopsis affects seed, causing cracking, shriveling, dull appearance, and gray mold on the seed surface; infected seedlings may be blighted, but no stem or root discoloration is described.
Phytophthora: Phytophthora produces a distinctive dark chocolate-brown discoloration of the lower stem extending several nodes upward from below the soil line, accompanied by brown/discolored roots, lower-leaf yellowing progressing upward, wilting, and leaves remaining attached after plant death.
Decision rule  : IF the diagnostic symptom is on the standing plant's lower stem — a dark chocolate-brown discoloration rising from the soil line through several nodes — THEN diagnose Phytophthora; IF the symptom is confined to the seed (cracked, shriveled, gray mold) with no such stem discoloration, THEN diagnose Phomopsis.
